This is Jadhima ibn Malik, one of the earliest Tanukhid kings of al-Hira, known by the titles al-Abrash and al-Waddah. The chroniclers say that al-Zabba’, queen of Palmyra, killed him in revenge for her father Amr ibn Zarib. See al-Tabari, vol. 2, p. 32.↩︎
The text is called the Namara inscription after the place where it was discovered, in the Hawran mountains of Syria.↩︎

This is Imru’ al-Qays I, one of the Lakhmid kings of al-Hira, known by the title al-Muharriq or Muharriq, a title later associated with Banu Nasr. al-Tabari says of this Imru’ al-Qays that he was one of the Persian governors and rulers over the frontier Arabs of Rabi‘a, Nasr, and others from the deserts of Iraq, the Hijaz, and the Jazira. al-Tabari, vol. 2, pp. 64–65.↩︎

Jurji Zaydan gives this clear Arabic rendering of the Namara inscription in History of Arabic Literature, Cairo, 1911, vol. 1, p. 28. The date at the end of the inscription follows the old Bosra calendar, which begins with Roman control of the Bosra region as a Roman province in 105 CE. Adding 105 to the number 223 written in the inscription gives 328 CE as the year of the death of Imru’ al-Qays I.↩︎

Lihyan and Thamud were two tribes or peoples—the word sha‘b, with a short i, means a large tribal group—living in western Arabia before the Common Era. Each established a local government after the collapse of Minaean and Sabaean rule in the Hijaz. Both used writing derived from the South Arabian Musnad script and spoke North Arabian dialects. As for the Safaitic people, their name comes from the al-Safa region of Syria, where Orientalists found ancient inscriptions. Similar inscriptions were also discovered elsewhere in the Syrian desert and upper Hijaz, and all were called Safaitic inscriptions after al-Safa to distinguish them from inscriptions named after other places where some of them were found.↩︎
The definite article al- was used in the following words in the inscription: al-Qays, al-Arab, al-taj, al-Asadayn—the two Banu Asad tribes—and al-shu‘ub, meaning the tribes.↩︎
The waw in sa‘adu marks the nominative among the Nabataeans.↩︎
The date recorded in the inscription is 463 according to the Nabataean calendar mentioned above. We must therefore add 105, giving the year 568 CE.↩︎

The Orientalist Margoliouth is known to have been the first to raise systematic doubts about pre-Islamic poetry, claiming that it had actually been composed during the Islamic period and then falsely attributed to pre-Islamic times. Taha Husayn followed him in this doubt and wrote his famous book On Pre-Islamic Poetry—later retitled On Pre-Islamic Literature after the well-known controversy—in an attempt to prove the claim.↩︎

Another reason should be added for the loss of some pre-Islamic poetry: Islam’s cautious attitude toward poetry that preserved pagan ideas or remnants of tribal fanaticism. Umar ibn al-Khattab was known to deal strictly with poets whose verse violated Islamic norms. It is also said that he increased the stipend of the poet Labid when he learned that Labid had stopped composing poetry. See Ibn Sallam, Classes of Poets, pp. 25, 30, 32, 42.↩︎

There is abundant historical evidence for this. One example is enough here. Ibn Sallam says of Quraysh that they looked at their share of poetry and found it small in the pre-Islamic period, so in Islam they increased it greatly. By “increased it,” he means that large amounts of poetry were fabricated and attributed to the pre-Islamic period. See Classes of Poets, p. 62; and the same source, p. 10.↩︎

See, for example, al-Aghani, Bulaq ed., vol. 1, p. 30. Abu al-Faraj tells the story of Ibn Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham asking Abd al-Aziz ibn Nahshal to compose verses praising Hisham ibn al-Mughira and attribute them to Nahshal, his father, as though he had recited them at Ukaz in the pre-Islamic period, in return for four thousand dirhams. Abu al-Faraj then gives the verses Abd al-Aziz ibn Nahshal composed for this purpose.↩︎
See Ibn Hisham, Life of the Prophet, vol. 1, pp. 18–26, 5–53, and elsewhere.↩︎

There are many examples showing that early scholars were aware of this problem. One is enough to stand for them all. al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi says that Hammad al-Rawiya corrupted Arabic poetry. He explains that Hammad knew the dialects of the Arabs, their poetry, the styles of their poets, and their meanings. Because of this knowledge, he could compose poetry closely resembling the style of an earlier, pre-Islamic poet, attribute it to that poet, and then spread it widely under that name. In this way, al-Dabbi says, the poetry of the Arabs became mixed together, and only a critical expert could distinguish the authentic from the false—and where could such an expert be found? See al-Aghani, Bulaq ed., vol. 5, p. 172.↩︎

Taha Husayn wrote in the introduction to the second edition: “This is last year’s book. One chapter has been removed, one retained, other chapters added, and the title has been changed slightly.” He did not explain what had been removed, retained, or added, or why the changes were made. In fact, what was removed was the first chapter on method. But the chapter was not really deleted except in two senses. First, it no longer appeared as the opening chapter. Second, certain phrases and words were changed, especially passages touching on some Islamic beliefs. The substance of the chapter, after revision, was divided between two new chapters: “Literature and Its History” and “The Pre-Islamic Arabs: Their Language and Literature.” He also added passages to the beginning and end of the chapter applying his method to some pre-Islamic poets, and added two chapters at the end of the book, one on the nature and forms of pre-Islamic poetry and one on pre-Islamic prose. These revisions were not made by his own free choice. He was forced into them after a campaign of intellectual and material intimidation led by rigid conservatives among Azhar scholars, university academics, and literary figures, along with members of the royal court pursuing political aims. Despite all of this, the basic argument and method of the book did not change.↩︎
